readerTitle: Same profit, different restaurant: which $100,000 is real?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당 두 곳 인수 비교, 소규모 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 이익은 크기보다 질을 먼저 본다. 내년에도 반복될 이익인가, 실제 현금으로 들어온 이익인가를 묻는다.
misconception: 이익이 같으면 두 사업의 가치도 같다. 이익이 늘었으면 사업이 좋아진 것이다.

sources.text: 재무 분석과 기업 인수 실사의 표준 개념 (이익의 질: 반복성, 현금 전환, 일회성 항목 구분)

factChecks.note: 식당 B 계산: 보고 이익 $100,000 − 일회성 보험금 $30,000 − 미룬 주방 수리 $15,000 = 반복 가능한 이익 $55,000. 그중 $25,000은 아직 받지 못한 케이터링 대금이라 현금으로 확인된 반복 이익은 $30,000. 모든 수치는 가상입니다.
소프트웨어 회사 계산: 이익 $200,000 → $600,000, 증가분 $400,000 = 일회성 맞춤 개발 $250,000 + 영업 인력 감축 절감 $100,000 + 신규 구독 $50,000. 합계가 맞는지 다시 확인했습니다.
'영업현금흐름과 이익을 여러 해 비교한다'는 일반적인 분석 관행으로 서술했습니다. 특정 기준치(예: 비율 몇 % 이상)는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Same profit, different restaurant: which $100,000 is real?
body: Two neighborhood restaurants are for sale. Each one made $100,000 in profit last year. Each owner asks the same price.
On paper, they're twins. A careful buyer would still pay very different amounts for them.

image.label: Two restaurant storefronts with identical profit signs
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 비슷한 동네 식당 두 곳이 나란히 있고, 각 창문에 똑같이 "$100,000 profit" 팻말. 한쪽 식당 뒤편에는 물이 샌 흔적과 쌓인 송장 더미가 살짝 보이도록. 실제 상호나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which restaurant would you pay more for?
body: **Restaurant A:** revenue flat for three years. Profit steady. Nothing unusual on the books.
**Restaurant B:** revenue up 15% thanks to a new catering business. The profit includes a line called "other income." The owner mentions the kitchen is "due for some work."

options.text: Restaurant A, because its profit looks steady
options.feedback: You give up B's growth story, but you get profit you can expect again next year. The next card shows what B's number hides.

options.text: Restaurant B, because it's growing faster
options.feedback: Growth is worth paying for when it's real and repeatable. Here you'd be paying for a number before checking what it's made of.

options.text: The same for both, since profit is equal
options.feedback: Fair as a starting point. But equal profit only means equal value if both profits will repeat and both arrived as cash.

cards.title: What Restaurant B's $100,000 is made of.
body: Only **$55,000** is likely to come back next year. And $25,000 of that hasn't been paid yet.

breakdown.label: Repairs put off
breakdown.detail: The bill will arrive next year

cards.title: Quality of earnings
body: **Quality of earnings** is how much of a reported profit is likely to happen again and actually turns into cash.

Two businesses can show the same profit with very different quality. Restaurant A's profit is plain, repeating and paid. Restaurant B's is padded by a one-off, flattered by skipped spending, and partly still owed.
Ask two questions of any profit: *Will it come back?* and *Did it arrive as money?*

image.label: Profit bar split into solid and hollow parts
image.brief: 가로 막대 두 개. 위는 "Restaurant A $100,000" 전체가 단단한 색. 아래는 "Restaurant B $100,000"인데 일부만 단단하고 나머지는 점선·반투명으로 "one-time", "put off", "not yet paid" 라벨.

cards.title: Where weak profit usually hides.
body: Most low-quality profit comes from three places:
list: **One-offs:** selling equipment, an insurance payout, a single huge order
**Money not yet collected:** sales recorded, but customers haven't paid
**Spending pushed off:** skipped repairs, paused marketing, a job left unfilled
cards.callout: A quick check: compare cash from operations with profit over several years. If cash keeps falling short, look closer.
cards.softwareNote: In a software business, watch for one-time setup or custom-build fees counted alongside subscriptions. Only the subscriptions are likely to repeat.

cards.title: Low profit can be high quality.
body: Quality works both ways. Imagine Restaurant A had shown only $70,000 because it replaced its walk-in fridge for $30,000 last year.
That expense won't repeat soon. Its underlying profit is still about $100,000, and a buyer who sees that can get a fair deal.
So the skill isn't suspicion. It's sorting each number into *this will happen again* or *this won't*.

cards.title: It takes judgment, not a formula.
body: "One-time" costs that show up every year aren't one-time. Be wary of anyone who removes a new one each year.
Cash can also lag profit for good reasons. A fast-growing business often has more unpaid invoices simply because it's selling more.
And cutting spending isn't always a trick. The question is whether the business can keep running well without it.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You're thinking of buying a small subscription software company. Its profit jumped from $200,000 to $600,000. The $400,000 increase came from three places.
Which part would you trust most to repeat?

options.text: $250,000 from a custom project built for one large client
options.feedback: It's the biggest piece and it's real money. But it only repeats if another client wants the same thing.

options.text: $100,000 saved by cutting the sales team from three to one
options.feedback: The saving will repeat. The cost may show up later as slower sign-ups, so check how new users are arriving.

options.text: $50,000 from 150 new monthly subscribers, with churn unchanged
options.feedback: The smallest piece, but the highest quality: it renews, it's paid monthly, and it can keep growing.

cards.title: Judge profit by what it's made of, not just its size.
body: Before you trust a profit number, yours or anyone's, ask whether it will come back next year and whether it arrived as cash.
**Try it today:** take last year's profit. Cross out anything that won't repeat and anything not yet paid. What's left is the number to plan around.
